title: Designing a Task — The TBLT Cycle

pts: Introduce the topic and task, activating relevant schema and vocabulary without pre-teaching the target language itself.
Over-preparing the pre-task risks turning the task into a rehearsed performance rather than genuine communication.
A short model or demonstration here clarifies the task's mechanics without scripting its content.

v: Two photos of a lost bag; a short teacher recording or a live demonstration

items: Show two photos of a school bag left on a bus and ask what might be inside.
Brainstorm topic words on the board, accepting home-language words and giving English equivalents.
Explain the task and its outcome: each group will write a lost-and-found notice that helps the owner get the bag back.
Demonstrate the mechanics with a volunteer: one learner describes a bag, the other asks questions.
Give the time limit and start the task.
Play a one-minute recording of two teachers doing a similar task (Willis 1996).
Support: a picture word bank on the board.
Challenge: groups must also include a way to check that the claimant is the real owner.

lines: T: What’s in this bag, do you think?
S1: Tiffin box.
S2: Geometry box. And… how to say ‘kannadaka’?
T: Spectacles. Or glasses. Good.
T: Your task: write a notice for the bus depot. The owner must be able to find the bag. You have ten minutes.

blocks.x: Activate topic words, but do not pre-teach the target structure (It has a…, It was left on…). Over-preparing turns the task into a rehearsed performance.

body: Figure 28.1 Open the door, don’t furnish the room

Purpose: to show the aim of the pre-task. Content: a teacher opening a door labelled ‘Topic’ and ‘Task’; behind it an empty room that learners are about to furnish themselves with their own words. Style: simple, symbolic. Board version: a door and a question mark.

items: Google Slides (free) for photos and task instructions.

blocks.x: A real bag with objects inside, or a quick board drawing.

pts: Learners complete the task in pairs or groups, focused on the outcome, with the teacher monitoring but not correcting.
This mirrors Unit 7's monitoring-without-interrupting principle applied specifically to task-based work.
Language accuracy is deliberately not the focus at this stage — meaning and outcome are.

v: A ranking task; a monitoring sheet for the teacher

items: Give groups of four a ranking task: choose the five most useful items for a two-day school trip to Hampi from a list of twelve.
Groups discuss and agree a ranked list.
Move round the room with a monitoring sheet; listen without correcting.
Note useful language, frequent errors and language learners seemed to need.
Intervene only if a group is off task or stuck completely.
Use a local problem instead: five ways to keep the school ground clean.
Support: pictures of the twelve items with names.
Challenge: groups must agree unanimously, with reasons for each choice.

lines: Good language heard: We can share one torch. / Water is more important than snacks.
Errors to revisit: more better / we will must take
Language needed: comparing (more useful than, the most important).

blocks.x: The teacher’s role during the task is to listen, not to teach. This applies the monitoring principle of Unit 7 to task-based work: meaning and outcome are the focus here, not accuracy.

body: Purpose: to show quiet monitoring. Content: groups talking on benches; the teacher leans towards one group, clipboard in hand, lips closed, noting. Style: calm, observational. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Keep (free) on a phone for quick notes while monitoring.

blocks.x: A clipboard with a three-column monitoring sheet.

body: In a class of fifty, you cannot hear every group. Choose four groups to monitor closely each lesson and rotate them. Over two weeks you will have listened to everyone.

pts: Learners prepare to report their task outcome to the class or another group, which raises attention to accuracy naturally.
This planning stage is where Skehan's trilogy shifts measurably toward greater accuracy and complexity.
Keep planning time brief and focused — its value comes from anticipation, not extended rehearsal.

v: Notebooks; a dictionary per group if available

items: Tell groups they will report their outcome to the class in one minute.
Groups agree what to say and choose a speaker.
They draft key sentences; the teacher moves round as a language adviser.
Give a brief rehearsal: the speaker practises once to the group.
Groups prepare a written report on chart paper instead of a spoken one.
Support: a report frame (We chose… because… We did not choose… because…).
Challenge: the speaker may not read from notes, only glance at keywords.

lines: We decided that water is the most important thing, because Hampi is very hot. We did not choose a phone because it can get lost.

blocks.x: Knowing that an audience is waiting raises attention to accuracy naturally, and planning time tends to shift performance towards greater complexity and fluency (Foster and Skehan 1996). Keep planning brief: its value comes from anticipation, not extended rehearsal. Unit 29 examines these effects in detail.

body: Purpose: to show the shift in attention. Content: a group at a bench; above them, a thought bubble moves from loose scribbles to a neat three-line report card. Style: light. Board version: a messy cloud and an arrow to a tidy box.

items: Vocaroo (free) for the speaker to record and hear one rehearsal.

blocks.x: Notebook drafts and a single rehearsal to the group.

pts: Groups report their outcomes to the class, creating a real audience and purpose for accurate, clear language.
This stage often surfaces the richest naturally-occurring errors for the following language-focus stage.
Keep teacher intervention minimal here too — this is still primarily a communicative stage.

v: Board space; a listening grid for the class

items: Give the class a listening grid: group, top choice, reason.
Four or five groups report; the others complete the grid.
Ask where groups agreed and disagreed, commenting on content first.
Note, silently, language points for the next stage.
With fixed benches, groups report to the group behind them instead of to the whole class, then one or two report publicly.
Support: the class listens for only one item of information.
Challenge: listeners ask each reporting group one question.

blocks.x: A listening grid (written for this book):

lines: Group 1: water, because it is hot. Group 2: first-aid kit, because someone may fall. Group 3: cap, because the sun is strong.
T: Interesting. Three groups chose water first. Group 2, why the first-aid kit?

blocks.x: The report gives a real audience and purpose for clear language, and it often surfaces the richest errors for the language focus. Keep intervention minimal; this is still a communicative stage.

body: Purpose: to show the report stage. Content: a learner reporting from the front; the class listening with grids on their desks, one hand raised. Style: warm, realistic Indian classroom. Board version: a grid with group numbers.

items: Mentimeter (free basic plan) for groups to post their top choice and see a class chart.

blocks.x: A tally of choices on the board.

points.sub: Now, and only now, the grammar
pts: Analyse language forms that emerged from the task, chosen based on what learners actually needed and used.
This inverts the traditional order — language focus follows communication, rather than preceding and constraining it.
This is where Unit 6's consciousness-raising and CCQs are most naturally deployed.

items: Write four or five sentences heard during the task and report, some correct, some not, without names.
Pairs decide which are correct and fix the others.
Focus on one form the learners needed (here, comparatives and superlatives).
Use concept-checking questions and a short consciousness-raising task (Unit 6).
Give brief practice, then ask groups to improve one sentence from their own report.
Learners find useful phrases in a recording of fluent speakers doing the same task (Willis 1996).
Support: underline the part of each sentence to check.
Challenge: learners find a second form they needed and research it.

lines: Water is more better than snacks. → Water is better than snacks.
The first-aid kit is the most important thing. (correct)
We will must take a cap. → We must take a cap.
T: Is water better than snacks, or the same?
Ss: Better.
T: So do we need ‘more’ as well?
Ss: No.

blocks.x: This inverts the traditional order: language focus follows communication rather than preceding and constraining it, and the forms chosen are the ones learners actually needed.

body: Purpose: to show language focus built on learner output. Content: a board with five sentences, two circled; a magnifying glass over more better; learners in pairs discussing. Style: clear, board-like. Board version: the sentences themselves.

items: Google Docs (free) for keeping a running list of errors from tasks across a term.

pts: A genuine task has a non-linguistic outcome and requires language use to reach it — a gap, a problem, a decision.
An 'activity' that only practises pre-specified language, with no real outcome, is not a task in this technical sense.
This connects to Unit 3's information-gap principle as one reliable way to generate a genuine task.

items: Choose five speaking or writing activities from the coursebook you use.
Test each against four questions (see model language).
Classify each as a task, a near-task or an exercise.
Convert one exercise into a task by adding a gap and an outcome.
In a teacher circle, each teacher converts one exercise and the circle trials all of them.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: 1. Is the main focus on meaning? 2. Is there a gap (information, reasoning or opinion)? 3. Do learners use their own language resources? 4. Is there a clear non-linguistic outcome?

blocks.x: An exercise converted (written for this book):

lines: Before: Ask and answer: What time does the train leave? It leaves at…
After: Pair A has the Bengaluru–Mysuru train timetable; Pair B has a list of three appointments in Mysuru. Together, choose the train that gets you to all three on time.

blocks.x: An activity that only practises pre-specified language, with no outcome, is not a task in this technical sense. Information gaps (Unit 3) and Prabhu’s reasoning gaps are two reliable ways to create one.

body: Purpose: to summarize task criteria. Content: a door labelled ‘Task’ with four locks, each labelled ‘Meaning’, ‘Gap’, ‘Own language’ and ‘Outcome’; a key ring beside it. Style: iconic, clean. Board version: four boxes with ticks.

body: Prabhu’s Bangalore project did not teach grammar explicitly at all. Its evaluation was debated, but the project shaped international thinking about tasks, and the term ‘reasoning gap’ comes from Prabhu’s own account (Prabhu 1987).

points.sub: Not just the language, the task
pts: Task difficulty can be graded by complexity of information, number of steps, and time pressure — not only by vocabulary level.
This gives a second lever for differentiation (Unit 15) beyond simplifying language alone.
A cognitively engaging task with familiar language often outperforms a linguistically 'graded' but dull one.

v: A simple town map in three versions

items: Version 1: learners give directions from the bus stand to the post office on a map with few streets.
Version 2: the same, but with more streets and two routes, one blocked by roadworks.
Version 3: plan a route that visits three places in the shortest time, with no pointing.
Groups choose the version that suits them, or the teacher assigns versions.
Add time pressure to Version 1 for a fluency push, or remove it from Version 3.
Support: Version 1 with a phrase card.
Challenge: Version 3 with a partner who has an out-of-date map.

blocks.x: Levers for grading a task (after Robinson 2001):

lines: More or fewer elements (streets, places, people).
One step or several steps.
Here-and-now (map in view) or there-and-then (from memory).
Time pressure or no time pressure.

blocks.x: The language, go straight, turn left, opposite the, stays the same; the thinking changes. This gives a second lever for differentiation (Unit 15) beyond simplifying language. A cognitively engaging task with familiar language often works better than a linguistically graded but dull one.

body: Purpose: to show task grading. Content: three maps of the same town, increasingly busy, with the same direction phrases beneath all three. Style: map style, pastel. Board version: three quick grids.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for drawing three map versions.

blocks.x: Hand-drawn maps, or a map drawn on the board with changes added.

pts: Skipping the language-focus stage wastes the diagnostic value the task cycle was designed to generate.
Over-correcting during the task itself collapses the fluency-focused purpose of that stage.
Choosing a task with no genuine gap or outcome quietly turns TBLT into a disguised traditional exercise.

Mark each pitfall as avoided, partly avoided or present.
Choose one pitfall to fix and plan the change.
Teach the lesson again with another class and compare.
Colleagues exchange recordings and review each other’s lessons (see Unit 68 on peer observation).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

dek: Unit 28 of 100: pre-task, task cycle, and language focus — the three-stage structure that turns task-based teaching from a slogan into a repeatable lesson design.

aims.x: This unit turns task-based language teaching (TBLT) from a slogan into a lesson design. It follows Jane Willis’s framework stage by stage (pre-task, task, planning, report and language focus) and then asks three practical questions: what counts as a task, how can tasks be made easier or harder, and where does the cycle usually go wrong?
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: set up a task without pre-teaching the language it will need;
monitor a task without interrupting it;
use planning and report stages to raise attention to accuracy;
run a language focus stage built on what learners actually said;
apply four criteria to decide whether an activity is a task;
grade task difficulty by changing the task, not only the language;
recognize the common pitfalls of TBLT and avoid them.

why: Why this matters. 'Task-based' is often used loosely to mean any activity. The actual TBLT cycle is a specific, disciplined structure — and its order is what makes it work.

background.x: Task-based teaching has deep roots in India. Between 1979 and 1984, N. S. Prabhu and a group of teachers in Bangalore and other South Indian centres taught English to school classes through problem-solving tasks, such as reading timetables or following directions on a map, with no grammar syllabus at all (Prabhu 1987). Prabhu’s argument was that grammar is best acquired when the mind is occupied with meaning. His reasoning-gap tasks, which require learners to infer or deduce something new from given information, are still among the most useful task types for school classes.

Later writers gave the idea a clearer shape. Jane Willis (1996) proposed a three-phase framework (pre-task, task cycle and language focus) that teachers could follow lesson by lesson. Rod Ellis (2003) set out criteria that distinguish a task from an exercise, and David Nunan (2004) distinguished real-world tasks, such as booking a ticket, from pedagogic tasks designed for the classroom. Michael Long (2015) argued for a syllabus built entirely from tasks learners need outside class. TBLT has also been criticized. Michael Swan (2005) argued that its claims go beyond the evidence and that it can neglect the systematic teaching of new language. Implementation studies have found teachers struggling with noise, home-language use and exam pressure (Carless 2004).

These concerns are real in Indian classes of forty to sixty with a year-end examination. The answer is to adapt the cycle: shorter tasks, clear roles, planned reports, and a language focus linked to the textbook. NCF 2023 calls for experiential, competency-based learning, and a well-run task cycle is a concrete way of providing it (NCERT 2023). Learners may use their home languages while planning; the report stage then gives a clear reason to move into English.

items: Outcome achieved. Check whether each group reached the task outcome, such as a usable notice or a ranked list.
Report quality. Assess reports for clarity, organization and appropriate language on a short rubric.
Language focus uptake. In the next task, listen for the forms taught in the language focus.
Teacher checklist. Use the pitfalls checklist once a month to review your own task lessons.
How much of your pre-task time goes on teaching the language the task will need?
What do you find hardest about not correcting during a task?
Which coursebook activities are real tasks, and which are exercises?
How could your learners report in a class of fifty without taking the whole lesson?
Where does home-language use help your task cycle, and where does it get in the way?
Which stage do you skip most often, and why?

terms.def: A stage in a lesson, especially at the end of a task cycle, where learners examine and practise language features that arose during the task (Willis 1996).
Watching and listening to learners while they work, to check understanding, give help, note language for later feedback and decide when to move on.
A task designed for classroom use that prepares learners for real-world tasks, involving meaning-focused communication, such as a map-reading information gap.
In task-based teaching, the stage before the main task that introduces the topic, activates vocabulary and may include planning or modelling.

A task that closely mirrors something people actually do outside the classroom, such as booking a ticket, writing a complaint or following directions. It contrasts with a pedagogic task, which is designed for learning but may not occur in everyday life.

A task in which learners derive new information from given information through inference, deduction or practical reasoning, such as working out a timetable from clues. The term comes from Prabhu’s Bangalore project (Prabhu 1987).

The stage of the task cycle in which groups prepare and present an account of how they did the task and what they decided or found, usually to the whole class. Planning the report pushes learners towards more accurate, public language (Willis 1996).

A meaning-focused activity in which learners use language to achieve a non-linguistic outcome, drawing on their own resources (Ellis 2003). Planning a class trip within a budget is a task; a drill of pre-specified sentences is not.

The cognitive demands a task makes on learners, shaped by features such as the number of elements, reasoning required and time pressure (Robinson 2001). Complexity can be raised or lowered to sequence tasks.
The central phase of a task-based lesson, in which learners do the task, plan a report and present it to the class (Willis 1996). It is preceded by a pre-task and followed by a language focus.
